newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ short end retains bid tone ahead of jobs data.
newsitem.headline: NZ short end retains bid tone ahead of jobs data.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 93.02 (PREV 92.99) 90-DAYS 6.76 (PREV 6.78)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.15 PCT (PREV 6.00) US 5-YR 6.53 (PREV 6.51)
* NZ bills bid ahead of March quarter employment data
* Bonds steady to slightly bid across curve
* Dealers watch for composition of qtrly employment growth
New Zealand's short end maintained its bid tone on Tuesday morning ahead of March quarter employment data, which the market hopes will confirm recent signs of a soft economy.

The 90-day bank bills opened a couple of pips lower at 6.76 percent, while the June futures contract was four stronger at 93.03 on good volume of 1,186 contracts. The overnight cash rate bumped up to 6.20 percent from 6.00 percent.

Bonds were steady to slightly bid right across the curve, with the 11/06 two basis points stronger at 7.72 percent following a bounce up to 7.74 percent at Monday's close after encountering resistance at 7.69 percent.
Dealers said flows would probably be calm ahead of Household Labour Force data at 10.45 a.m. (2245 GMT).

Economists polled by Reuters expect on average March quarter employment growth of 0.35 percent, although forecasts range from 0.1 percent to 0.7 percent. Employment growth was negative 0.5 percent in the previous quarter.
The unemployment rate is forecast to rise to 6.2 percent from 5.9 percent.

Dealers said quarterly employment growth on or below the average forecast would be consistent with the view that the economy troughed in the December quarter, as employment lagged the economy by around three months.

A Wellington dealer said the market would be watching closely for the break-down between part time and full time employment, as the December quarter's 0.5 percent fall in growth had been driven largely by a drop in the number of part time jobs.
"The composition once again is important in this number. If we see the part time jobs scream up, and the full time jobs remain flat, that is not as inflationary as perhaps first thought," he said.
-- Catherine McCaw, Wellington newsroom (64 4) 471 4275
